entry: System of partial differential equations describing the motion of viscous fluids. The equations are named after Claude-Louis Navier and George Gabriel Stokes, who developed them from 1822 (Navier) to 1842–1850 (Stokes); [[Siméon Denis Poisson]] independently reached the same results. They express [[Momentum|momentum]] balance for Newtonian fluids using the [[Conservation of mass|conservation of mass]], and generalize the Euler equations, which consider only inviscid flow. The equations model aircraft and car design, blood flow, power station design and [[Pollution|pollution]], and, coupled with [[Maxwell's equations]], form the basis of magnetohydrodynamics. The Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem asks whether solutions in three-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] remain smooth and bounded, or break down into unbounded ones. It is one of seven [[Millennium Prize Problems]], for which the Clay Mathematics Institute offered $1 million prizes in 2000. In September 2026 OpenAI announced a claimed counterexample; the claim, followed by a priority dispute, has yet to be independently verified.

Branch of a state's armed forces designated for [[Naval warfare|naval]] and amphibious warfare. A navy conducts combat on lakes, rivers, coasts and [[Ocean|oceans]], using surface ships, amphibious ships, [[Submarine|submarines]] and seaborne aviation. Its offensive role is projecting force beyond a country's shores, for example to protect sea-lanes, confront [[Piracy|piracy]], ferry troops or attack other navies, ports and shore installations. Its defensive role is to frustrate such projection by enemies, and it may include nuclear deterrence through submarine-launched ballistic missiles. Before cannon were carried aboard ships, combat centered on ramming and boarding, as in [[Ancient Greece]] and the [[Roman Empire]], where oared vessels such as triremes were built to sink enemy ships. China's first official standing navy was established in the [[Song dynasty]] in the 12th century. Navies are often described as brown-water (riverine and littoral), blue-water (open-ocean) or green-water (in between), distinctions based more on strategic scope than on tactical division.

Salvadoran politician, president of El Salvador since 2019. After being ousted from the Farabundo Martí National Liberation Front in 2017, he founded Nuevas Ideas and won the presidency with 53 percent of the vote. His Territorial Control Plan and a 2022 gang crackdown led to more than 85,000 arrests; homicides fell from 38 per 100,000 people in 2019 to 1.9 in 2024, a figure whose accuracy has been contested. He made [[Bitcoin|bitcoin]] legal tender in 2021. Critics describe [[Censorship|press censorship]] and a 2020 episode in which 40 soldiers entered the legislature, described by the opposition as a self-coup.

Largest city in the Northern District of [[Israel]] (pop., 2024: 75,704). Known as "the Arab capital of Israel", it is a cultural and religious center for Arab citizens. Its inhabitants are predominantly Arabs, of whom 69% are Muslim and 31% Christian. The New Testament describes Nazareth as the childhood home of [[Jesus]], and it has been a center of [[Christianity|Christian]] pilgrimage. The Church of the Annunciation, considered one of the largest Christian sites of worship in the Middle East, commemorates the Annunciation. The town became important during the [[Crusades]], when Tancred made it capital of the Principality of Galilee.

German state (1933–45) under [[Adolf Hitler]] and the [[Nazi Party]], officially the German Reich and later the Greater German Reich. The Nazis claimed succession to the Holy Roman Empire and German Empire and called their state the Third Reich, or Thousand-Year Reich, but it lasted 12 years. After Hitler became chancellor in 1933, the party eliminated opposition and centralized power in his person. Heavy military spending, public works and secret rearmament, financed by deficit spending, ended mass unemployment. Hitler's territorial demands included the [[Anschluss]] of Austria in 1938 and the seizure of the Sudetenland region of Czechoslovakia; the invasion of Poland in 1939 began [[World War II]] in Europe. Racism and antisemitism were central to the regime, which persecuted [[Jews]], Slavs and Romani people; its racial policies culminated in the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]]. After invading the [[Soviet Union]] in 1941, Germany lost the initiative in 1943 and capitulated in May 1945.

Far-right German political party (1920–45) that created and supported [[Nazism]]. Officially the National Socialist German Workers' Party (NSDAP), it grew from the German Workers' Party (1919–20) and drew on Freikorps paramilitary culture. It had little popular support until the Great Depression. Under [[Adolf Hitler]], its leader from 1921, it sought to segregate and eventually exterminate [[Jews]], [[Slavs]] and others, a campaign that culminated in the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]]. After President [[Paul von Hindenburg]] appointed Hitler chancellor on January 30, 1933, the party established a totalitarian regime. It was declared illegal after Germany's defeat in [[World War II]].

System of internment camps operated by [[Nazi Germany]] from 1933 to 1945. The first camps opened in March 1933, soon after [[Adolf Hitler]] became chancellor. After the 1934 purge of the SA, the [[Schutzstaffel|SS]] alone ran them. Early prisoners were mostly communists, but the camps later held "habitual criminals," "asocials" and [[Jews]], and from the start of World War II, people from German-occupied Europe. There were more than a thousand camps and subcamps, and from 1941 a separate system of extermination camps was dedicated to murder. About 1.65 million people were registered prisoners, and about a million died, most in the second half of the war. Liberation came in 1944 and 1945, but hundreds of thousands died on death marches. Many Germans approved of the camps while they operated, in part because Nazi propaganda depicted prisoners as dangerous criminals.

Far-right, ultranationalist and totalitarian ideology associated with [[Adolf Hitler]] and the Nazi Party, formally named National Socialism. It is a form of [[Fascism|fascism]] that emphasizes pseudo-scientific racial hierarchy, identifying ethnic Germans and Nordic-Aryans as a master race. Nazism opposes liberal democracy and advocates dictatorship, [[Antisemitism|antisemitism]], anti-communism and [[Eugenics|eugenics]]. It aimed to create a racially homogeneous society and to gain land for expansion under the doctrine of *Lebensraum*. It rejected Marxist class conflict and universal equality, and *Mein Kampf* outlined Hitler's antisemitism and his *Führerprinzip* (leader principle). During World War II, millions, including two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population, were exterminated in the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]]. After Germany's defeat, Nazism became widely regarded as evil. Only fringe groups, usually called [[Neo-Nazism|neo-Nazis]], describe themselves as its followers, and use of Nazi symbols is illegal in many European countries.

Burmese general and politician who was military dictator of Burma from 1962 to 1988. Ne Win founded the Burma Socialist Programme Party and led the 1962 [[Coup d'état|coup d'état]] that overthrew the parliament of U Nu, establishing a one-party socialist state under the Burmese Way to Socialism. He served as head of government in 1958–60 and 1962–74, and as head of state from 1962 to 1981. His rule was marked by a non-aligned foreign policy, isolationism, one-party rule and economic stagnation. He resigned in July 1988 after the 8888 Uprising, and the military State Law and Order Restoration Council replaced his party. He was later placed under house arrest. Relations with [[China]], broken between 1967 and 1971 over Chinese support for insurgents and anti-Chinese riots, were restored in March 1971.

Extinct group of archaic humans, *Homo neanderthalensis*, of Europe and Western and Central Asia. Neanderthals lived there during the Middle to Late Pleistocene and died out in most of their range by about 40,000 years ago, perhaps as early modern humans arrived. They survived longer in parts of the [[Iberian Peninsula]]. The first recognized [[Fossil|fossil]] was found in 1856 in the Neander Valley, Germany. Males averaged about 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) and 75 kg (165 lb). Brain volume averaged 1,640 cc (100 cu in) in males and 1,460 cc (89 cu in) in females, higher than any living human population, although its organization differed in areas linked to cognition and language. A 2010 genome showed interbreeding with modern humans, and people of non-African descent carry small amounts of Neanderthal ancestry. Neanderthals made Mousterian stone tools, maintained fire, possibly wore blankets and ponchos, and buried their dead.

Landlocked state in the [[Great Plains]] of the U.S. (pop., 2020: 1,961,504), capital Lincoln. Admitted in 1867, two years after the [[American Civil War]], it has a unicameral legislature whose members are elected without party labels. The west is treeless prairie with a semi-arid climate, while the east is humid. Violent [[Thunderstorm|thunderstorms]] and [[Tornado|tornadoes]] occur mainly in spring and summer. Indigenous peoples, including the Omaha, Pawnee and Lakota, lived in the region for thousands of years before European exploration. The Transcontinental Railroad and the Homestead Acts brought rapid settlement in the 1870s and 1880s, and agriculture remains central.

Second king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, reigning 605–562 BC. Often called Nebuchadnezzar the Great, he was the longest-reigning king of his dynasty, ruling for 43 years. As a commander he led armies in the Medo-Babylonian conquest of the Assyrian Empire and, at the Battle of Carchemish in 605 BC, defeated an Egyptian army under Pharaoh Necho II. In the 580s BC he campaigned against rebellious vassals in the [[Levant]]. He besieged [[Jerusalem]] in 587 BC, destroying it and the Kingdom of Judah, and deported much of its population in the [[Babylonian captivity]]. He also captured the [[Phoenicia|Phoenician]] city of Tyre. As a builder he erected many of [[Babylon]]'s religious buildings, including the Esagila and Etemenanki, and renovated its processional street and the Ishtar Gate.

Luminous part of the [[Interstellar medium|interstellar medium]], made of ionized, neutral or molecular [[Hydrogen|hydrogen]] and cosmic dust. The word is Latin for "cloud, fog". Nebulae are often star-forming regions, such as the Pillars of Creation in the [[Eagle Nebula]]. There, gas and dust clump into denser regions that collapse into [[Star|stars]], and the remaining material may form planets. Most are hundreds of light-years across and far less dense than a vacuum made on Earth, although the densest reach 10⁴ molecules per cubic centimeter. Many glow through fluorescence from embedded hot stars; others are visible only with long exposures. The [[Orion Nebula]] is the brightest nebula in the sky and can be seen with the naked eye. Originally the term covered any diffuse object, including the [[Andromeda Galaxy]], until [[Edwin Hubble]] and others confirmed the nature of galaxies in the early 20th century.

Model of how the [[Solar System]] formed from gas and dust orbiting the Sun. It is the most widely accepted model in cosmogony, and proposes that the planets accreted from this material. [[Immanuel Kant]] published the theory in 1755, and [[Pierre-Simon Laplace]] modified it in 1796. The modern solar nebular disk model explains features such as the nearly circular, coplanar orbits of the planets. Stars form in giant [[Molecular cloud|molecular clouds]], and a protoplanetary disk typically forms around each young star. A Sun-like star takes about 1 million years to form, and its disk evolves into a planetary system over 10–100 million years. Dust grains coagulate into kilometer-sized planetesimals, which merge into terrestrial planets. [[Giant planet|Giant planets]] form beyond the frost line and accrete hydrogen–helium gas once they reach 5–10 Earth masses. [[Uranus]] and [[Neptune]] are thought to be failed cores that formed too late.

Paraphilia involving sexual attraction to, or acts with, corpses. Also called necrophilism and thanatophilia, it is classified as a paraphilia by the [[World Health Organization]] and the American Psychiatric Association. Motives vary, from sexual domination of a non-responsive partner to fetishization of death and bereavement of a sexual partner. The DSM-5-TR can diagnose recurrent, intense sexual interest in corpses as Other Specified Paraphilic Disorder when it causes marked distress or impairment. Animal necrophilia, or Davian behavior, is usually attributed to an inability to distinguish a receptive mate from a recently dead one.

Racing video game franchise published by [[Electronic Arts]]. Most entries are arcade racers centered on illegal street racing and police pursuit, though some are simulations or focus on legal circuit races. The first title, *The Need for Speed*, appeared in 1994, and the most recent mainline title, *Need for Speed Unbound*, on December 2, 2022. The series was originally developed by Distinctive Software in [[Vancouver]], [[British Columbia]], before Electronic Arts bought the company in 1991. The franchise had sold over 150 million copies by October 2013 and has spawned a film and licensed Hot Wheels toys.

Queen of [[Ancient Egypt]], great royal wife of Pharaoh [[Akhenaten]] in the 18th Dynasty. With her husband she promoted Atenism, an exclusivist religion centered on the sun disc that may have been monotheistic, and their reign was arguably the wealthiest period of Egyptian history. After Akhenaten's death, some scholars believe she briefly ruled as the [[Pharaoh|pharaoh]] Neferneferuaten before [[Tutankhamun]] came to the throne, but this remains debated. Her painted bust, excavated in the early 20th century from the buried studio complex of the sculptor Thutmose, is in Berlin's Neues Museum. It is one of the most copied works of ancient Egyptian art.

Real number that is less than zero, usually written with a minus sign. Negative numbers are the opposite of positive real numbers and represent losses, deficiencies and [[Debt|debts]], as well as temperatures below zero on the [[Celsius]] and [[Fahrenheit]] scales. The laws of arithmetic ensure that the opposite of an opposite returns the original value: −(−3) = 3. Every real number other than zero is either positive or negative, while zero has no sign. Negative numbers appear in the Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art, which in its present form dates from the [[Han dynasty]] (202 BC–AD 220). By the 7th century, Indian mathematicians such as [[Brahmagupta]] described their use, and Islamic mathematicians developed the rules for subtracting and multiplying them. [[Diophantus]] considered negative solutions "false," and Western mathematicians such as Leibniz held that they were invalid but still used them.

Failure to exercise the care expected in similar circumstances. In [[Tort|tort]] law, negligence is harm caused by violating a duty of care through a negligent act or failure to act. A plaintiff must generally establish that the defendant owed a duty, breached it and caused harm, and that the plaintiff suffered [[Damages|damages]], though some jurisdictions recognize three elements and others five. Losses may include physical injury, property damage, psychiatric illness and economic loss. The modern law dates from *Donoghue v Stevenson* (1932), in which a woman who found a decomposed snail in a bottle of ginger beer sued the manufacturer, because privity barred a [[Contract|contractual]] claim. Lord Atkin defined a "neighbour" as a person so closely affected by one's acts that one should reasonably have them in contemplation. In England, *Caparo Industries Plc v Dickman* (1990) set a three-part test of foreseeability, proximity and what is fair, just and reasonable.

Geographically localized [[Community|community]] within a larger town, city, suburb or rural area, sometimes a single street and the buildings lining it. Neighborhoods are often social communities with considerable face-to-face interaction. Researchers lack an exact definition, but one describes a neighborhood as a specific geographic area and a set of social networks in which residents share values and maintain social control. Most ancient and historical cities had neighborhoods, which in some preindustrial traditions handled protection, upkeep and the regulation of births and marriages informally, as in Islamic cities. Ethnic, religious and economic groups often clustered in particular neighborhoods, and migrants tended to move in with relatives. Neighborhood sociology studies local life, and some scholars view the neighborhood as a small-scale [[Democracy|democracy]] regulated by reciprocity among neighbors.

[[Australia|Australian]] television [[Soap opera|soap opera]] (1985–2025). Created by Reg Watson, it is set in Erinsborough, a fictional suburb of [[Melbourne]], and centers on Ramsay Street. The Seven Network cancelled it four months after it began in 1985, and Network Ten commissioned a second season. It became the longest-running drama series in Australian television history in 1997. It was sold to more than sixty countries and was especially popular in the United Kingdom, where it began on [[BBC]] One in 1986. It was revived in 2023 after a 2022 cancellation, and its final episode aired in December 2025.

American astronaut and aeronautical engineer, first person to walk on the Moon. As commander of [[Apollo 11]] in 1969, he and [[Buzz Aldrin]] landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969. Stepping onto the surface, Armstrong said, "That's one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind," a broadcast seen live by an estimated 530 million viewers. He was a naval aviator in the [[Korean War]], flying from an [[Aircraft carrier|aircraft carrier]], and later a test pilot at the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, where he flew the North American X-15. In March 1966 he commanded Gemini 8, which made the first docking of two spacecraft before it was aborted to stabilize a dangerous roll. After leaving NASA in 1971 he taught at the University of Cincinnati until 1979 and served on the Rogers Commission investigating the [[Space Shuttle Challenger disaster]].

American singer-songwriter, one of the best-selling musicians in history. He has sold more than 56.5 million records in the United States alone. He wrote and recorded 10 singles that reached No. 1 on the U.S. Billboard Hot 100 and Adult Contemporary charts, including "Cracklin' Rosie" and "Song Sung Blue." 38 of his songs reached the Adult Contemporary top 10, including "Sweet Caroline." He starred in the 1980 musical drama *The Jazz Singer*. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2011 and received a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2018.

English author of short fiction, novels, comic books, audio theatre and screenplays. His works include the comic series *The Sandman* (1989–1996) and the novels *Good Omens* (1990), *American Gods* (2001), *Coraline* (2002) and *The Graveyard Book* (2008). *The Graveyard Book* was the first work to win both the Newbery and Carnegie medals. Beginning in 2024, numerous women published sexual assault accusations against him, and one accuser sued him and his estranged wife Amanda Palmer for [[Rape|rape]] and [[Human trafficking|human trafficking]]. Gaiman has denied the allegations, and several adaptations of his work were affected or halted.

Canadian and American singer-songwriter and musician. Born in [[Toronto]], he began his music career in [[Winnipeg]] in the 1960s and moved to Los Angeles in 1966 to form Buffalo Springfield. Known for distorted guitar playing with Crazy Horse, he earned the nickname "Godfather of Grunge" and recorded the 1995 album *Mirror Ball* with [[Pearl Jam]]. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1995 as a solo artist and in 1997 with Buffalo Springfield. He has advocated environmental causes and sustainable agriculture, and co-founded Farm Aid in 1985.
